title: Why You Can't Tickle Yourself
sources: Self-produced touch feels less ticklish because the brain (cerebellum) predicts the sensory consequences of your own movement and attenuates them (Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith 1998, Nature Neuroscience 1:635; Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith 2000, NeuroReport)
The same touch delivered by someone else is rated as more ticklish (Weiskrantz, Elliott & Darlington 1971, Nature; Blakemore et al. 1998)
Using a robot interface, adding a delay of 200 ms between the person's own movement and the touch made it feel significantly more ticklish (Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert 1999, J Cogn Neurosci 11:551)

lines.text: Try to tickle yourself right now. It doesn't work, does it?
lines.caps: Try to *tickle | *yourself | right now | It doesn't *work | does it?

lines.text: Your brain predicts every move your own hand makes.
lines.caps: Your *brain | *predicts | every move | your own *hand makes

lines.text: So it cancels the feeling before it even arrives.
lines.caps: So it *cancels | the feeling | before it | even *arrives

lines.text: That's why someone else's tickle hits so much harder.
lines.caps: That's why | *someone else's | tickle hits | so much *harder

lines.text: But here's the twist. Scientists built a tickle robot to trick the brain.
lines.caps: But here's | the *twist | Scientists built | a *tickle robot | to *trick the brain

lines.text: Add a delay of just a fifth of a second, and your own tickle starts to work.
lines.caps: Add a *delay | of just | a *fifth of a second | and your own tickle | starts to *work

lines.text: So, are you ticklish? Tell me in the comments.
